sentence: It does not stop the spread of these infections to other people either.
For most infections, people start to feel better after a few days.
The NHS says treatment is best started as soon as the first signs of infection appear.
The NHS also advises avoiding kissing and oral sex while a cold sore is present, to reduce the risk of passing on the infection.
The NHS lists headache, dizziness, feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, stomach ache, rash, itching, tiredness and fever as possible effects of the tablets and liquid.
If dizziness or faintness occurs, the NHS advises not driving, cycling or using machinery until it passes.
Creams and eye ointment are less likely to cause side effects.
Some people get mild burning or stinging that usually goes away quickly.
The skin can react to sunlight, so the NHS suggests staying out of bright sun and avoiding sun lamps and sun beds.
Serious effects are rare.
They include a serious allergic reaction, liver problems, kidney problems and changes in blood cells.
Swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or difficulty breathing, can be signs of a serious allergic reaction and need a 999 call.
For a side effect that is still bothering someone, the NHS suggests speaking to a doctor or pharmacist.
The NHS says most adults and children can take aciclovir.
It may not be suitable for someone who has had an allergic reaction to aciclovir or to valaciclovir, a similar medicine.
The prescriber may adjust the treatment for people with kidney problems, people over 65 and children.
People with a weakened immune system, such as those with HIV or a bone marrow transplant, may be advised about the best type of aciclovir.
Tablets may be recommended rather than the cream for them.
The NHS says aciclovir can usually be used in pregnancy, but a pharmacist or doctor is asked first.
Cream or ointment can usually be used while breastfeeding if the baby does not touch the treated areas.
A person who is breastfeeding is asked to tell the doctor before taking tablets.
The NHS says certain medicines may not mix well with some types of aciclovir tablets.
Examples named are cimetidine, mycophenolate mofetil and probenecid, with aminophylline and theophylline also listed.
No medicines are known to affect aciclovir cream or eye ointment.
The NHS advises telling a doctor or pharmacist about any other medicines, herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.
It says there is not enough information to show that herbal remedies and supplements are safe to take with aciclovir.
These products are not tested in the same way as pharmacy and prescription medicines.
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk during treatment, and food and drink are not restricted.
This applies to the tablets and the other forms alike.
No treatment removes the herpes virus from the body completely.
MedlinePlus says acyclovir does not cure cold sores or genital herpes and may not stop the spread to other people.
What it does, according to the NHS, is stop the virus multiplying and spreading, which helps the immune system deal with the infection.
